Airmen assigned to the 388th Aircraft Maintenance Squadron’s 4th Aircraft Maintenance Unit at the 388th Fighter Wing, Hill Air Force Base, Utah, work together to perform engine maintenance. (U.S. Air Force photos by Staff Sgt. Zachary Rufus)
WASHINGTON — The Air Force is walking back an award announcement it made in error for a massive contract vehicle worth up to $16.1 billion for propulsion work, a service spokesperson told Breaking Defense.
On Nov. 20, the Air Force announced it had picked 58 companies for the service’s Advanced Propulsion Acquisition Contract (APAC), set to run through 2041. The program is structured as an indefinite delivery, indefinite quantity contract, meaning the Air Force is not necessarily obligated to spend its full amount.
That award, published on the Pentagon’s daily contract roundup, was posted erroneously, an Air Force spokesperson confirmed today, though the service is planning to eventually award the contract. After the disclosure to Breaking Defense, the Pentagon subsequently noted the correction in the Nov. 23 list of award announcements.
“Once awarded, APAC will serve as an agile, enterprise-level contracting vehicle for propulsion requirements across all lifecycle phases, including science and technology, research and development, test and evaluation, production, sustainment, and modernization,” the Air Force said in a statement to Breaking Defense.
The Air Force additionally confirmed that a total of 58 vendors so far are planned for selection, and that an initial $1,000 disbursement to each will “support participation” in a post-award orientation conference for the winners.
“Future orders will be competed among the qualified vendor pool as requirements are validated and funded. Specific platforms, scope, funding, contract type, period of performance, and pricing will be established at the individual Delivery Order or Task Order level,” the statement reads.
The vendor pool from the Nov. 20 contract notice features a range of firms, from startups to established engine primes with different areas of propulsion expertise. And the award comes as the Air Force seeks new and more effective ways to power its existing and future platforms, from drone wingmen to large mobility aircraft.

该指南意义重大且必要，因为驻扎在美国大陆的军事单位必须能够自由地将其人员和资源运送到港口、铁路和机场，以便在危机期间在全球范围内部署。为这些装置提供动力并支持设备运输的关键基础设施系统越来越多地受到对手的攻击。

“当敌人或自然灾害破坏市政电网、供水系统或光纤干线时，任务会立即感受到。这就是为什么今天的峰会和新的 DCI 社区协调指南在作战层面至关重要，”上周在刘易斯-麦科德联合基地举行的第二次陆军主导的关键基础设施防御峰会后，第一军团指挥官马修·麦克法兰中将告诉记者。 “今天下午，我们与州、地方、公用事业和港口合作伙伴并肩坐下来演练太平洋西北地区的部署场景，绘制我们共同的依赖关系图，并在危机发生之前确定运营障碍。”

Army publishes guidebook for defending critical infrastructure at local installations - Breaking Defense
A rainbow over the Port of Tacoma in Tacoma, Washington, US, on Tuesday, March 4, 2025. (David Ryder/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
WASHINGTON — The Army has published a first-of-its-kind “playbook” to help installations develop plans and coordinate with stakeholders for the defense of their critical infrastructure systems.
The Defense Critical Infrastructure Community Coordination Guide was published last week, in coordination with the Army, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, FBI, Environmental Protection Agency, Department of Transportation, Department of Energy, and the Federal Emergency Management Agency.
The guide is significant and needed because military units based in the continental United States must be able to freely get their people and resources to ports, rails and airports in order to deploy around the globe during a crisis. Increasingly, the critical infrastructure systems that power these installations and enable the ferrying of equipment are under attack by adversaries.
To make matters worse, many of those systems are owned and operated by private companies and local municipalities, not the federal government or the military.
“When an adversary or natural disaster disrupts a municipal power grid, a water system, or a fiber trunk, the mission feels it immediately. That is why today’s summit and the new DCI community coordination guide are vital at the operational level,” Lt. Gen. Matthew McFarlane, commander of I Corps, told reporters following the second Army-led Defense of Critical Infrastructure summit at Joint Base Lewis-McChord last week. “This afternoon, we sat shoulder to shoulder with our state, local, utility, and port partners to walk through a Pacific Northwest deployment scenario, map our shared dependencies, and identify operational barriers before a crisis ever hits.”
The idea of developing a playbook was teased at the first summit at Fort Bragg in May, with the goal of creating a repeatable process to replicate across the country in order to be more prepared when an incident occurs.
We’re “very excited to have the community coordination guide. That’s something we’re hoping will continue to be scaled across the Army footprint and arguably among our colleagues across the Department of War,” Brandon Pugh, principal cyber advisor to the Secretary of the Army, told reporters.

content:
是的，不，也许？能够（或不能）交付乌克兰要求的 40 架 F-16 的国家 - Breaking Defense
2025 年 8 月 21 日，南达科他州乔福斯机场，第 114 战斗机联队的一架 F-16 战斗机在加力启动的情况下开始夜间飞行行动。（美国空军国民警卫队军士长卢克·奥尔森摄）
米兰和贝尔法斯特——上周，当俄罗斯无人机和导弹如雨点般袭击乌克兰领土时，总统弗拉基米尔·泽伦斯基恳求欧洲国家元首提供更多 F-16 来保卫国家——并给出了非常具体的数量。
“我们现在拥有的 F-16 ......花了很多时间进行维修而不是飞行。所以我们需要更多的战斗机。更多的 F-16 ......我感谢我们空军联盟中的每个国家。已经做了很多工作，但我们需要做得更多。具体来说，我们还需要 40 架 F-16，”泽连斯基周二在第 37 次乌克兰国防联络小组 (UDCG) 会议上以 Ramstein 格式表示。
这就提出了两个问题：首先，为什么是 40？其次，哪些国家能够现实地交付这么多飞机？
虽然乌克兰政府没有公布其航空武器库的官方清单，但航空出版物 AeroCorner 援引开源数据库估计，截至 2026 年 9 月，乌克兰拥有 39 架 F-16AM 战斗机。据报道，到 2025 年底，这些飞机执行了该国空军约 80% 的出动架次，包括所有任务类型。 （FlightGlobal 的 World Air Force 2026 目录显示乌克兰拥有 35 架较旧的 F-16A 型号；鉴于乌克兰信息的不透明性，两个数据集之间的微小差异是有道理的）。
对于泽连斯基的观点，总部位于伦敦的皇家联合军种研究所最近发​​布的一份报告强调了包括 F-16 在内的西方战斗机在击落俄罗斯无人机方面的作用。如果这些飞机被迫执行该任务，则意味着乌克兰可能在其他地方使用的昂贵和稀有资产会受到严重磨损。因此，基辅寻求将其机队规模扩大一倍是有道理的——尽管这可能并不容易。
乌克兰国防部没有回应就为何 40 架喷气式飞机成为目标的置评请求。欧洲政策分析中心的国防分析师费德里科·博尔萨里 (Federico Borsari) 告诉 Breaking Defense，虽然 40 架飞机是一个“合法的要求”，但这也是一个“雄心勃勃的庞大数字，而且在乌克兰获得它们绝对不容易，尤其是在短时间内”。
那么，它们从哪里来呢？显而易见的答案是首先关注 F-16 最大运营商（也是唯一生产商）的美国。然而，除了一些无法使用的机身外，华盛顿一直不愿意向乌克兰提供自己机队中的战斗机。因此，基辅将再次关注其欧洲支持者。

Yes, no, maybe? The countries that can (or can't) deliver Ukraine's 40 requested F-16s - Breaking Defense
An F-16 Fighting Falcon from the 114th Fighter Wing launches into night flying operations with the afterburner engaged at Joe Foss Field, S.D., Aug. 21, 2025. (U.S. Air National Guard photo by Master Sgt. Luke Olson)
MILAN and BELFAST — Last week, as Russian drones and missiles rained down on Ukrainian territory, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy pleaded with European heads of state for more F-16s to defend the country — with a very specific number.
“The F-16s we have now… spend a lot of time being repaired instead of flying. So we need more fighter jets. More F-16s… I’m grateful to every country in our Air Force Coalition. A lot has already been done, but we need to do more. Specifically, we need 40 more F-16s,” Zelenskyy said at the 37th Ukraine Defense Contact Group (UDCG) meeting on Tuesday in the Ramstein format.
That raises two questions: First, why 40? Second, which countries could realistically deliver this many aircraft?
While the Ukrainian government does not publish an official inventory of its aerial arsenal, the aviation publication AeroCorner, citing open-source databases, estimated that as of Sept. 2026, Ukraine possesses 39 F-16AM Fighting Falcons. It reported that by the end of 2025, these aircraft were flying around 80 percent of all the country’s Air Force sorties, including all mission types. (FlightGlobal’s World Air Force 2026 directory says Ukraine has 35 of the older F-16A models; a small discrepancy between the two datasets makes sense given the opaque nature of information out of Ukraine).
To Zelenskyy’s point, a recent report published by the London-based Royal United Services Institute emphasized the role of Western fighter jets, including the F-16s, to shoot down Russian drones. If the jets are forced into service for that mission, it means heavy wear and tear on expensive and rare assets that Ukraine could be using elsewhere. Hence, Kyiv seeking to roughly double its fleet makes sense — though likely won’t be easy.
The Ukrainian Ministry of Defense did not respond to a request for comment on why 40 jets is the target. Federico Borsari, a defense analyst with the Center for European Policy Analysis, told Breaking Defense that while 40 planes were a “legitimate request,” it was also “an ambitious, big number and definitely not easy to get them in Ukraine, especially in a short period of time.”
So, where could they come from? The obvious answer would be to look first to the United States, the largest operator (and sole producer) of the F-16. However, aside from some non-operational airframes, Washington has been unwilling to provide Ukraine with fighter aircraft from its own fleet. So Kyiv will instead look once more to its European supporters.

According to the ubiquitous tracker F-16.net, at the time of writing, eight European countries (outside Ukraine) operate or are introducing the fighter jets into active military service, and three others — Norway, the Netherlands, and Denmark — have retired them.
After Tuesday’s meeting, only Belgium was officially listed as willing to provide F-16s—10 by the end of the year. Brussels announced back in 2024 that it would eventually give Ukraine 30 F-16s as the military transitions its fighter fleet to the F-35, also made by Lockheed Martin. According to FlightGlobal’s directory, Belgium has 52 F-16s (44 F-16AMs and 8 F-16BMs) and is expected to reach full operational readiness of its F-35 fleet in 2030 (ordered 34 F-35As and plans to acquire 11 more).
As for any additional F-16s, Bosari said that even if European countries agree to send planes to Ukraine, several factors would make such deliveries complex in the short term, from the need to modernize some jets to reactivate retired ones, secure third-party transfer authorization (as with Belgian F-16s), and complete lengthy maintenance work.
There may also be a time crunch for Zelenskyy, Borsari said, thanks to upcoming elections in some European nations are another factor likely to affect or complicate potential fighter deliveries.
“In some countries, such as France, [which pledged at the UDCG meeting to send two Mirage 2000-5F to Ukraine by the end of 2026], where elections are coming up, it might be more complex to justify these transfers in the eyes of the population. I’m not saying it won’t happen, but there is a political dimension to these agreements that are also politically sensitive in some nations,” the expert said.
Three European countries operating F-16 fighter jets — Greece, Slovakia, and Poland — have scheduled national parliamentary elections in 2027.
Here is what to know about the state of the rest of Europe’s F-16 fleets.
Nearly five years after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, several European nations appear to be at a crossroads, asking themselves whether they can release any operational fighter jets without weakening or altogether putting at risk their own air forces.
While most countries didn’t immediately respond to Zelenskyy’s 40-plane request, Portugal went ahead and ruled out sending F-16 jets to Ukraine, with Portuguese Foreign Minister Paulo Ranger calling such a transfer “essentially impossible” during a press conference in Kyiv last week because the country needs its existing aircraft to protect its own territory.
Greece, one of Europe’s largest F-16 operators, received about 170 fighter jets in different configurations between the 1990s and 2010 and has since undergone a major modernization program. But it has maintained its decision not to transfer any aircraft to Kyiv, opting instead to focus on helping to train Ukrainian pilots and technicians.
Norway retired its F-16 fleet in 2022 after more than 40 years of service, sold 32 to Romania and has already donated six to Ukraine. But the Norwegian Ministry of Defense told Breaking Defense no other F-16s will be forthcoming.
“The remaining [F-16] airframes are not assessed as viable to return to operational service and will be used for purposes such as maintenance training and museum display,” the ministry said.
The Undeclared, And The Unlikely
At this week’s Ramstein meeting, Denmark committed €200 million ($218 million) for air defense and a €645 million package of drones and F-16 ammunition, but did not say whether it would send more F-16s to Kyiv than it already promised. The Scandinavian country has previously said it would transfer up to 19, with the first deliveries made in 2024.
Romania has spent significant effort building its F-16 fleet, which represents the only combat-ready jets the country has, relied on for air policing across the Black Sea. At the same time, it waits for its own F-35 deliveries, expected to start in the early 2030s. As such, it is not likely to be in a position to transfer a significant number of fighters. Romania’s defense ministry did not respond to a request for comment at press time.
Since the onset of the war, Turkey, which possesses the second-largest F-16 fleet in all of NATO, has not publicly committed to send any of its aircraft to Ukraine, focusing rather on drone and armored vehicle donations. The Turkish MoD did not provide comments on the matter at the time of writing.
Slovakia received its full fleet of new F-16 Block 70 fighters this year and ordered four additional ones in September to replace the aging MiG-29s it sent to Ukraine in 2023. But since then, Slovakia’s stance has hardened as the current government has halted most military assistance to Kyiv. The Slovak Ministry of Defense did not respond to a request for comment at press time on whether this remains its position.
Similarly, Poland has previously opted to transfer MiG-29s rather than its F-16s to Ukraine. In 2023, Wojciech Skurkiewicz, Secretary of State at the Ministry of National Defense, told the Polish Parliament that “there was no discussion about handing over F-16 aircraft to the Ukrainian side.” It remains unclear whether this decision has changed. The Polish MoD did not respond to a request for comment at press time.
The Netherlands retired its F-16 in 2024 and completed deliveries of its 24 pledged jets to Ukraine a year later. The country has also supported Kyiv by providing retired aircraft for training and, in February, announced plans to supply F-16 simulators. However, it appears the Dutch have no F-16s left to send to Kyiv, having handed 18 to a training center in Romania for a symbolic one-euro sum in November 2025. The Dutch defense ministry did not respond to a request for comment at press time.
Bulgaria has ordered F-16 Block 70 jets, but local reports note that a delay to a second batch of eight aircraft has led Sofia to explore options for a second-hand fighter jet. The Eastern European country’s political support for military aid supplies to Ukraine is waning, with Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev reportedly stopping weapons and ammunition transfers because of budgetary issues. The country’s MoD did not respond to a request for comment at press time.

# 'Maintain control': UN chief calls for creation of global AI safety framework within a year

UN chief Antonio Guterres on Monday urged countries to agree on the creation of a global framework for managing the dangers posed by artificial intelligence within one year. Speaking at a summit in Barbados, he warned that taming the technology is vital if humanity is to stay in charge of its own future.

 File photo: UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres is shown delivering a speech. © Ted Aljibe, file photo via AFP

[UN](https://www.france24.com/en/tag/united-nations/) Secretary-General [Antonio Guterres](https://www.france24.com/en/tag/antonio-guterres/) called Monday for the world's nations to adopt a mechanism to temper the risks posed by [AI](https://www.france24.com/en/tag/artificial-intelligence/), as he addressed a conference on the technology in [Barbados](https://www.france24.com/en/tag/barbados/).

As the end of Guterres's time at the helm of the international body approaches, he has become increasingly vocal about the need for AI safety measures to avoid a future in which "[killer robots](https://www.france24.com/en/technology/20261120-countries-open-to-international-pact-on-killer-robots-after-un-talks)" are a reality.

Read more[Nations agree to talks on regulating 'killer robots' by 2028](https://www.france24.com/en/technology/20261120-countries-open-to-international-pact-on-killer-robots-after-un-talks)

"Today I call for member states to coordinate efforts and to develop within the next year a globally inclusive and principles-based multilateral framework for AI risk management, backed by independent and credible oversight," he said.

## 'Control of our world'

International regulation of AI appears little more than a pipe dream as the technology's superpowers, the [United States](https://www.france24.com/en/tag/usa/) and [China](https://www.france24.com/en/tag/china/), seek the upper hand in research and development breakthroughs.

Nonetheless, Guterres said that a starting point could be for countries to agree on shared safety measures, a testing regime and basic requirements for independent oversight.

In September, [Anthropic](https://www.france24.com/en/tag/anthropic/) CEO Dario Amodei, [OpenAI](https://www.france24.com/en/tag/openai/) CEO Sam Altman and [SpaceX](https://www.france24.com/en/tag/spacex/) chief [Elon Musk](https://www.france24.com/en/tag/elon-musk/) called for a [slowdown](https://www.france24.com/en/americas/20260923-ai-leaders-urge-caution-at-un-with-anthropic-chief-pledging-to-slow-down) on the development of AI.

Read more[AI leaders urge caution at UN, with Anthropic chief pledging to slow down](https://www.france24.com/en/americas/20260923-ai-leaders-urge-caution-at-un-with-anthropic-chief-pledging-to-slow-down)

Others, like [Nvidia](https://www.france24.com/en/tag/nvidia/) CEO [Jensen Huang](https://www.france24.com/en/tag/jensen-huang/) and [Meta](https://www.france24.com/en/tag/meta/) CEO [Mark Zuckerberg](https://www.france24.com/en/tag/mark-zuckerberg/), want to move full steam ahead.

Regulators in the US, where AI development has proceeded at the fastest pace, are unlikely to intervene.

In September, US President [Donald Trump](https://www.france24.com/en/tag/donald-trump/) hosted a group of American tech executives who agreed to abide by a voluntary code of conduct on AI safety.

Guterres said Monday at the Bridgetown Special Summit On AI Safety that "when one looks at different other institutions of global governance ... they correspond to the reality of the world in 1945."

"It's clear that institutions need to be reformed in order to adapt themselves to the realities of today's world," he said in response to an AFP question.

"That applies to the UN, and that applies to the international financial architecture, that applies to the world trade system."

Guterres said that he would advise his successor, due to take office in the New Year but yet to be selected, that properly controlling AI would be necessary for "humanity to maintain control of our world".

华盛顿——来自华盛顿海军区 (NDW) 的 45 名人员参加了海军设施司令部 (CNIC) 指挥官事件管理小组/危机行动小组成员课程，这是 11 月 18 日至 19 日举行的为期两天的虚拟培训。

CNIC 为来自 NDW、中大西洋海军区、日本海军区、东南海军区和西南海军区 5 个地区 21 个基地的 120 多名学员进行了培训。该课程为分配到安装事件管理团队和区域危机行动团队的人员提供了共同的基础。

CNIC IMT/CAT 会员课程 CIN S-540-1040/CDP 25B1 是后续现场紧急行动中心/事件管理团队培训师课程的先决条件。讲师介绍了事件指挥系统、国家事件管理系统、作战中心程序、指挥官意图、通用作战图开发以及指挥、控制、通信、计算机和情报套件 (C4IS) 工具。

对于 NDW，培训帮助人员了解自己的角色并在紧急情况下协调信息、行动和建议。
NDW 地区应急管理项目总监 Greg Powe 表示：“事件管理团队/危机行动团队成员课程帮助华盛顿海军区 CAT 成员建立一个管理紧急情况的通用操作框架：了解他们的角色、保持态势感知、跨组织协调以及为指挥官提供及时的决策支持。”

Powe 表示，每个 NDW 设施都会派 IMT 成员参与，帮助建立整个地区的深度。

鲍威说：“我希望团队能够从本课程中获得的最大收获是在压力下作为危机行动团队的一部分发挥作用的实际能力，将快速发生的紧急情况转化为有组织的信息、协调一致的行动以及向领导层和支持合作伙伴提供的明确建议。”

讲师们强调，危机管理需要在紧急情况发生之前就进行深思熟虑的计划。

“应急管理不应该是一场临时游戏；而是一场规划游戏，”CNIC 海岸运营培训小组的课程讲师道格·比斯利 (Doug Beasley) 说。 “我们希望人们坐下来，了解他们的威胁是什么，他们的弱点是什么，他们如何相互合作，经历爬行、行走、跑步阶段，并确保他们知道他们需要知道的事情。”
虚拟形式允许参与者探索共同的挑战，包括标准化事件指挥系统原则如何应用于当地计划、危险、指挥关系和互助协议。
 以安装为主导的演习、熟悉紧急行动中心以及后续的现场团队课程使人员能够根据当地情况应用企业基础。

对于安装级别人员，该课程提供了有关专业部门如何融入更广泛的事件管理框架的背景信息。

“这让我对危机应对有了更全面的了解，”华盛顿海军支持活动舰队和家庭支持中心综合初级预防劳动力主管丽贝卡·劳埃德 (Rebecca Lloyd) 说。 “我曾在现实世界的紧急家庭援助中心担任临床角色，这次培训让我了解了危机应对行动的其他关键部分。”

劳埃德表示，该课程强调了了解其他团队的角色和保持良好关系的重要性。

WASHINGTON — Forty-five personnel from across Naval District Washington (NDW) participated in the Commander, Navy Installations Command (CNIC) Incident Management Team/Crisis Action Team Member Course, a two-day virtual training held Nov. 18-19.

CNIC conducted the training for more than 120 participants from 21 installations across five regions: NDW, Navy Region Mid-Atlantic, Navy Region Japan, Navy Region Southeast and Navy Region Southwest. The course provided a common foundation for personnel assigned to installation Incident Management Teams and regional Crisis Action Teams.

The CNIC IMT/CAT Member Course, CIN S-540-1040/CDP 25B1, is a prerequisite for the follow-on, on-site Emergency Operations Center/Incident Management Team trainer course. Instructors covered the Incident Command System, National Incident Management System, operations center procedures, commander's intent, common operating picture development and Command, Control, Communications, Computers and Intelligence Suite (C4IS) tools.

For NDW, the training helps personnel understand their roles and coordinate information, actions and recommendations during an emergency.

“The Incident Management Team/Crisis Action Team Member Course helps Naval District Washington CAT members build a common operating framework for managing emergencies: understanding their roles, maintaining situational awareness, coordinating across organizations, and providing timely, decision-ready support to commanders,” said Greg Powe, NDW region emergency management program director.

Powe said each NDW installation sent IMT members to participate, helping build depth across the region.

“The biggest takeaways I hope the team can gain from this course is a practical ability to function as part of a Crisis Action Team under pressure, converting a fast-moving emergency into organized information, coordinated actions, and clear recommendations for leadership and supported partners,” Powe said.

Instructors stressed that crisis management requires deliberate planning long before an emergency occurs.

“Emergency management shouldn't be a pickup game; it’s a planning game,” said Doug Beasley, a course instructor with the CNIC Shore Operations Training Group. “We want people to sit down, understand what their threats, their vulnerabilities are, how they can work with each other, go through that crawl, walk, run phase, and make sure that they know the things that they need to know.”

The virtual format allowed participants to explore shared challenges, including how standardized Incident Command System principles apply to local plans, hazards, command relationships and mutual-aid agreements.
 Installation-led drills, Emergency Operations Center familiarization and the follow-on on-site team course enable personnel to apply the enterprise foundation in local conditions.

For installation-level personnel, the course provided context on how specialized departments integrate into the broader incident management framework.

“It gave me a better whole picture view of crisis response,” said Rebecca Lloyd, supervisor, Integrated Primary Prevention Workforce, Fleet and Family Support Center, Naval Support Activity Washington. “I have participated in a real-world Emergency Family Assistance Center in a clinical role, and this training allowed me to see the other critical parts of crisis response operations.”

Lloyd said the course reinforced the importance of understanding the roles of other teams and maintaining strong relationships with tenant commands.

“No two crisis responses are the same, and the importance of not making assumptions and strictly going off past training scenarios and standard operating procedures was a major lesson,” Lloyd said.
 The virtual IMT/CAT Member Course convenes approximately 22 times annually. It establishes individual proficiency before participants advance to local drills, tabletop exercises and team-level operations center training.

By investing in continuous emergency management training, NDW strengthens its ability to support personnel, preserve critical infrastructure, and maintain mission readiness across the National Capital Region.

2032年快讯：中国的齐射未能击败台湾，北京陷入消耗战 - 大西洋理事会
2018 年 4 月 12 日，中国人民解放军 (PLA) 海军的军舰和战斗机参加在南海举行的军事展示。（路透社/斯金格，来自Reuters Connect）
本文是斯考克罗夫特中心印度-太平洋安全倡议系列“下一场战争的快报”的一部分，其中我们的专家对世界下一场重大冲突可能在最有可能爆发的地区印度-太平洋地区进行了假设。这些消息被称为虚构情报，或“FicInt”，在军队内部使用，让政策制定者为可能的未来做好准备。目的是防止下一场战争爆发。
2032 年，台北——中国第一批导弹和无人机在夜深人静时飞越台湾海峡。有些在咆哮的火焰喷射的推动下划过黑色的天空，而另一些则安静地、几乎看不见地以稳定的速度在黑暗的天空中嗡嗡作响。第一个被拦截导弹击中中国火柱摧毁，其他则在被激光闪光击中时爆炸。有些被小型拦截无人机撞到一边。一些人被自动炮和机枪的火幕击落，曳光弹在黑暗中摸索着目标，越来越多的条纹。
这些联合火力打击——中国对台战争中所宣称的第一次攻击——旨在摧毁台湾的防御，使其军事力量丧失能力，并粉碎台湾人的战斗意志。尽管这些齐射令人恐惧且令人印象深刻，但它们未能实现中国的目标。
一些袭击成功了，坠入港口、机场和军事基地，并向天空喷出滚滚火焰和浓烟。北起台北，南至高雄，台湾一次又一次遭到无情的打击。虽然台湾军事力量的来源是中国的目标，但许多平民也因这次袭击而被屠杀。世界领导人最初等着看台湾是否能够承受住这场冲击，或者是否会像许多分析人士预测的那样迅速崩溃。
但事实证明，台湾的多层防空和导弹防御系统“T-Dome”出乎意料地有效。尽管该公司在 2027 年首次投入运营时（即 2025 年宣布成立两年后）面临性能困难，但其许多自主系统的可靠性迅速成熟。随着中国入侵台湾领空和侵略性海上骚扰的行为年复一年变得更加频繁和充满敌意，台湾的总统和指挥官们更加放心地相信T-Dome允许自主攻击其认定的敌对目标。
尽管中国在发动袭击之前发起了旨在破坏台湾指挥和控制系统的强大网络攻势，但台湾慷慨地使用了 Anthropic 的 Claude Mythos 等前沿人工智能 (AI) 网络安全模型，发现并修补了几乎所有潜在的攻击向量，从而保持了 T-Dome 和其他系统的运行。对人工智能抱有如此大的信心的争议是不可避免的。战时的防御效果则不然。
T-Dome 证明了这些高风险决策的正确性，在第一轮拦截中拦截了 90% 的中国弹药。这为台湾指挥官赢得了宝贵的时间来分散兵力，使中国更难瞄准他们，采取预先计划

Dispatch from 2032: After Chinese salvos fail to defeat Taiwan, Beijing is trapped in a war of attrition - Atlantic Council
Warships and fighter jets of the Chinese People's Liberation Army (PLA) Navy take part in a military display in the South China Sea on April 12, 2018. (REUTERS/Stringer via Reuters Connect)
This article is part of “Dispatches from the Next War,” a series from the Scowcroft Center’s Indo-Pacific Security Initiative in which our experts provide hypothetical accounts of what the world’s next major conflict could look like in the region where it’s most likely to break out: the Indo-Pacific. These dispatches are styled as fictional intelligence, or “FicInt,” which is used within the military to prepare policymakers for possible futures. The aim is to prevent the next war from ever unfolding.
TAIPEI, 2032—China’s first missiles and drones flew across the Taiwan Strait in the dead of night. Some coursed across the black sky propelled by growling jets of flame, while others quietly and near-invisibly hummed through the dark sky at a steady pace. The first were destroyed by interceptor missiles snaking into Chinese columns of fire, others exploded when hit by flashes of laser light. Some were knocked aside by tiny interceptor drones. A few were downed by curtains of autocannon and machine-gun fire, with the growing streaks of tracer bullets groping for targets in the dark.
These joint firepower strikes—the vaunted first attack of China’s war on Taiwan—were meant to smash Taiwan’s defenses, incapacitate its military force, and shatter the Taiwanese will to fight. While these salvoes were terrifying and impressive, they failed to achieve China’s objectives.
Some of the attacks got through, crashing into ports, airfields, and military bases, and sending plumes of flame and smoke into the sky. From Taipei in the north to Kaohsiung in the south, Taiwan was mercilessly hit again and again. While sources of Taiwanese military power were China’s target, many civilians were also slaughtered by the attack. World leaders initially waited to see whether Taiwan could withstand the onslaught or whether it would quickly fold as many analysts had predicted.
But the T-Dome, Taiwan’s multi-layered air- and missile-defense system, proved unexpectedly effective. While it faced performance difficulties when it first became operational in 2027, two years after its announcement in 2025, the reliability of many of its autonomous systems matured rapidly. As China’s incursions into Taiwan’s airspace and aggressive maritime harassment grew more frequent and hostile year after year, Taiwan’s presidents and commanders became more comfortable putting greater faith in the T-Dome’s permission to autonomously engage targets it identified as hostile.
And while China’s strikes were preceded by a robust cyber offensive aimed at disrupting Taiwan’s command-and-control systems, Taiwan’s generous use of frontier artificial intelligence (AI) cybersecurity models like Anthropic’s Claude Mythos had discovered and patched nearly every potential attack vector, keeping the T-Dome and other systems operational. The controversy about placing so much faith in AI was inevitable; the defensive results in wartime were not.
The T-Dome vindicated those high-risk decisions, intercepting 90 percent of Chinese munitions in the first barrage. This bought Taiwan’s commanders precious time to disperse their forces and make it more difficult for China to target them, take up preplanned fighting positions across their nation, and start fighting back.
Further, the survivability and resilience of many Taiwanese bases, stations, and command posts proved to be highly robust. Many were built underground and were well-protected by dozens of meters of earth and rock. Missile after missile and drone after drone slammed into the vicinity of these underground command posts. While some were disrupted, as antennas were toppled and wiring cut, most remained operational.
Notably, Taiwan’s air force was able to maintain aviation command and control from its underground airbase within Toad Mountain, contributing both to air defense and strike missions of its own. Above-ground targets in Taiwan, such as airfields and main supply routes, were initially cratered and some aircraft were destroyed. But Taiwanese engineers repaired airfields, roads, and bases with alacrity. As a result, such hits resulted only in temporary pauses in Taiwan’s operations and did not amount to debilitating knock-out blows.
With most of its forces intact, Taiwan counter-attacked, firing its own munitions at key targets across mainland China. Many of these were intercepted. But due to the superior quality and reliability of Taiwan’s munitions, and China’s years-long strategic emphasis on offensive rather than defensive capabilities, a disproportionate number of Taiwanese munitions hit their marks.
In addition, the United States, Japan, and other nations provided Taiwan with exquisite intelligence and provided non-attributable, non-kinetic cyber and space capabilities that greatly enhanced the hit-rate of Taiwan’s defensive counterstrikes. Consequently, Taiwan devastated targets such as the ports where China’s amphibious forces were assembling, crippling the invasion before it even got underway. Chinese aviation command-and-control nodes and over-the-horizon radars were also hammered, giving Taiwan’s air force greater freedom of maneuver than most analysts had ever predicted.
The effects on Taiwanese morale were immeasurable. As with the US military’s famous Doolittle Raid on Japan after Pearl Harbor, the physical damage Taiwan inflicted on China was less important than the political and psychological results of Taiwan’s demonstrated resilience. Taiwan was not helpless, and the People’s Republic of China was not an invincible juggernaut.
With the quick, decisive campaign China had envisioned to isolate and invade Taiwan thwarted, the joint firepower strikes pressed on. Days dragged into weeks. Taiwan began running dry on interceptors, cannons began to jam, and even lasers began to burn out. Taiwan was forced to absorb more direct hits from Chinese strikes, even as China’s own magazines ran low.
If the war were evaluated today based on targets hit, the assessment would find that China has a commanding lead. But even with Taiwan’s dwindling munitions, the forces still in the fight have proven disproportionately effective. As the United States painfully experienced during Operation Epic Fury in Iran, even a greatly diminished adversary can still hold the advantage if it fights asymmetrically and selectively. While short on missiles, Taiwan has maintained plenty of launchers and conducted carefully sequenced strikes layered with joint operations and allied intelligence support that continue to bloody China’s nose. China’s Eastern Theater Command has still refused to launch an invasion fleet across the strait, as the mere preservation of Taiwan’s stand-in forces held the amphibious force at risk, making the amphibious invasion appear infeasible.
China—and the world—also grossly underestimated Taiwanese resolve. Despite polling that showed Taiwanese willingness to fight as even higher than that of Ukrainians prior to the Russian invasion in 2022, many analysts were skeptical that Taiwan would hold fast under the pressure of a Chinese offensive. Such analysts had focused primarily on the correlation of forces and means between China and Taiwan, weighing their assessments on numeric comparisons of ships, jets, and missiles available to both sides. This, however, failed to account for qualitative differences in Chinese and Taiwanese systems and societies, or for fundamental human elements that have always characterized the conduct of war. While bombing alone was not China’s plan, China had been as yet unable to launch its amphibious invasion because it could not set the necessary conditions. Bombing alone has never produced capitulation, and it has not here in Taipei.
Moreover, China’s narrative warfare and United Front activities, its strategic co-opting of domestic groups, had also penetrated swaths of Taiwanese society and foreign discourse, influencing pre-war public commentary to give a dim view of Taiwanese will and an overinflated view of Chinese prowess. The extreme pro-unification wing of the Kuomintang, the Chinese Nationalist Party in Taiwan, aligned itself with Beijing before the war. A few American commentators had advocated strategic restraint, isolationism, and nativism, while some American politicians echoed these sentiments, leading many to presume Taiwan would surrender at the first blush with its enemy.
But as with the staunch resolve of Ukrainians, it appears the Taiwanese are prepared to fight for years if necessary to preserve the democracy and way of life they built after ending martial law in 1987. Under attack, as they have seen their people killed in the streets, the Taiwanese have bravely rallied, pro-unification extremists have been politically isolated, and public sentiment in favor of taidu, formal Taiwanese independence, has skyrocketed. Civil-defense initiatives and energy-diversification efforts, which had been maturing for years, have also mentally prepared the population and the entire society to be resilient despite the immediate imposition of incredible hardship across the country.
Beijing now faces a dilemma. Backing down could deal a fatal blow to the credibility of the Chinese Communist Party, while pressing on would mean doubling down on sunk costs and putting the government’s dream of national rejuvenation further out of reach. Caught in a trap of its own making, China has looked abroad to Russia and North Korea for other solutions, while the Central Military Commission has begun to consider limited nuclear strikes to turn the tide in China’s favor.
Magazine depth cuts both ways. Taiwan may run low on munitions first in a future conflict, but even Chinese inventories are not limitless. And because China cannot hit everything at once, it will likely have to focus on high-priority targets, yielding maneuver space for Taiwanese forces.
Range rings also cut both ways. Taiwan falls within the range of most Chinese strike capabilities. China, too, is within range of many of Taiwan’s strike capabilities. If Taiwan is attacked by China, Taiwan will strike back at targets in China—not just at munitions or forces entering Taiwanese territory.
The earth is the most reliable and affordable shield. Interceptors are necessary, but they can be expensive and can quickly run dry under constant barrage. While difficult to scale, subterranean fortifications reduce reliance on interceptors and mitigate China’s ability to effectively target Taiwan’s forces.
Regardless of when, why, and how China may start the fight, the result would likely be a protracted war with Taiwan. Beijing may intend—and pundits may predict—a quick surrender by Taipei, but this is unlikely. There are many “roads to war” and rationales Beijing will claim led to its aggression, and many ways the war might begin, including a quarantine, a blockade, or outright attack. Regardless, China is unlikely to win rapidly or easily, almost inevitably leading to a protracted and costly conflict—if Taiwan continues its defense and resilience efforts.
Even successful strikes rarely deliver knockout blows, and an active defense can prove resilient even under sustained strike campaigns. Defenders will disperse to preserve forces and capabilities, and can rapidly repair airfields, ports, and bases.
When nations are attacked, cohesion surges, even among politically divided states. Blood calls for blood, defenders rally to their flag, and the will to fight becomes stronger than ever.
Third parties are not easily intimidated into total non-participation in wars that impact them. When nations can pursue their interests and frustrate their adversaries at low risk, they will.

Chinese v American Views on WAR with Taiwan
Posted Aug 14, 2026 by Martin Armstrong |
The Center for Strategic and International Studies conducted an extraordinary survey of 64 leading experts on China, Taiwan, and cross-Strait relations, including 28 former senior U.S. government officials, 23 former government policy and intelligence analysts, and 13 academics and think-tank experts. What their answers reveal is not that China is preparing to invade Taiwan tomorrow, as the neocons would like everyone to believe, but that Beijing remains willing to wait so long as nobody crosses the line of formal Taiwanese independence. Some 84% said Beijing is willing to wait for unification but will not accept the status quo permanently, while only 10% believed China seeks unification at the earliest opportunity. Not one of the 64 experts believed Beijing would ever accept an independent Taiwan.
This is precisely why Taiwan has become so dangerous. The West keeps portraying the conflict as if Xi Jinping wakes up every morning staring at a calendar trying to decide when to launch an amphibious invasion. Yet 83% of these experts said China did not plan to use significant kinetic force against Taiwan by 2027, and 80% said China’s enormous 2022 military exercises did not indicate Beijing had accelerated its timetable. Only 6% of respondents outside the former senior government group saw 2027 as a hard deadline, while not one former senior U.S. official did. The obsession with 2027 has nevertheless become extremely useful for the military establishment because every supposed deadline becomes another justification for weapons, deployments, bases, and spending.
The survey found that 44% believed Beijing has a hard deadline of 2049, the centennial of the People’s Republic, while 42% believed China could wait indefinitely provided unification remains possible. This is an important distinction because China thinks in terms of generations while Western politicians think in terms of the next election. Beijing does not need to invade Taiwan if economic, political, and military pressure can gradually change the situation in its favor. Only 20% of those surveyed believed China even possessed a coherent roadmap for peaceful unification, which tells us this is not some perfectly scripted invasion plan sitting in Xi’s desk drawer.
Where the numbers become alarming is not an unprovoked invasion but what happens when politicians begin crossing China’s red lines. More than three-quarters of the experts, 77%, believed China would invade within six months if Taiwan formally declared independence. Among former senior U.S. officials, that number was 79%. Even some of those who did not expect an immediate invasion believed Beijing would respond with a blockade or enormous military exercises. This is why politicians encouraging Taiwan toward formal independence are playing with the lives of 23 million people. They can deliver all the speeches they want about democracy from Washington, London, or Brussels, but they will not be the civilians sitting underneath the missiles if their political experiment goes wrong.
Not one expert believed an explicit American commitment to defend Taiwan would cause China to invade immediately, but 64% believed Beijing would respond strongly enough to provoke a U.S.-China or China-Taiwan crisis, while another 31% expected a more limited negative response. Only two of the 64 experts believed formally committing America to Taiwan’s defense would actually deter China from using force because Beijing already assumes that the United States will intervene anyway.
A direct invasion is not even the most likely path toward conflict. Only 8% of the experts described an amphibious invasion within ten years as likely, while 63% called it possible and 27% unlikely. Force short of invasion received much higher probabilities, with 52% saying deliberate escalation such as a blockade was likely or very likely. An accidental military incident was considered even more dangerous, with 34% saying a collision or accident around the Taiwan Strait was likely and another 22% calling it very likely. When warships and aircraft from opposing nuclear powers continually operate around the same small body of water, war does not require some grand master plan. It requires one mistake followed by politicians who refuse to back down.
A later CSIS survey of American and Taiwanese experts reinforces that point. Roughly 90% of U.S. experts and 62% of Taiwanese experts believed China already possessed the capability to impose a law-enforcement-led quarantine that substantially reduces trade into Taiwan. Around 80% of American experts and 60% of Taiwanese experts believed Beijing could execute a PLA blockade, while Taiwanese experts were considerably more skeptical that China could successfully carry out an invasion. If Beijing wanted to coerce Taiwan during the following five years, experts considered a quarantine the most likely option. If China decided it wanted immediate unification, however, approximately 80% regarded a highly kinetic joint blockade as likely or very likely.
This is where the economic consequences become enormous because Taiwan does not need to be invaded for the world economy to be thrown into chaos. A quarantine or blockade would immediately threaten shipping, insurance, semiconductor supply chains, electronics, automobiles, communications equipment, and virtually every modern industry dependent upon advanced chips. The later CSIS survey found most American and Taiwanese experts did not believe Taiwan could withstand a Chinese blockade for longer than three months without substantial U.S. intervention. Washington would then face the decision nobody wants to discuss honestly: accept China’s blockade or attempt to break it militarily and risk direct war between two nuclear powers.
Taiwan is also the world’s semiconductor pressure point. The island’s importance to advanced chip manufacturing means a serious blockade would not remain a regional event. Factories thousands of miles away could discover that a conflict they thought had nothing to do with them suddenly prevents them from obtaining critical components. Markets would begin repricing the risk immediately, shipping premiums would explode, companies would scramble for inventory, and governments would discover once again how fragile global supply chains have become. This is why capital will react long before politicians formally declare that a war has begun.
What I find particularly revealing in the later CSIS survey is the difference between American confidence and Taiwanese confidence in Washington. An astonishing 96% of American experts were completely or moderately confident that the United States would intervene militarily if China invaded Taiwan during the following five years. Taiwanese experts were less confident in American intervention and considerably less confident that U.S. allies would join the fight. It is always easier for people thousands of miles away to be certain about somebody else’s war.
This is precisely why Taiwan remains one of the critical geopolitical pressure points as we move toward 2029. The danger is not simply that China arbitrarily decides to invade. The greater danger is escalation, miscalculation, political promises that cannot be withdrawn, and Western policymakers convincing themselves that every additional provocation somehow produces deterrence. China has made its position on formal independence perfectly clear, and even the experts inside the Western foreign-policy establishment overwhelmingly acknowledge that Beijing would react with force if that line were crossed.
If Taiwan declares formal independence, 77% of the experts surveyed believed China would invade within six months. That is not a statistic policymakers should treat as another war-game scenario. It is a warning about what happens when politicians deliberately remove the ambiguity that has helped keep the peace.

content:
【大紀元2026年11月24日訊】（大紀元記者鍾又淳報導）11月22日，香港藝人陳慧琳出席香港馬場活動並跳唱演出。受訪時她透露，17歲長子劉昇（蝦餃仔）即將離港升學。她還分享，自己用AI分析未來兒媳的趣事。
陳慧琳與富商丈夫劉建浩2008年結婚，育有兒子劉昇和劉琛。陳慧琳向來作風坦率且寵愛兒子，每次出席公開活動接受訪問時，記者都會例行關心兩名兒子的近況。由於17歲的長子「蝦餃仔」劉昇正值高中畢業、準備升讀大學的關鍵階段，自然成為媒體追問的焦點。
現在距離明年8月長子離港赴海外升學的日子越來越近，陳慧琳坦言，一想到要與兒子分隔兩地便十分不捨，甚至預告送機時會「喊到變豬頭」（哭成淚人兒）。她直言「還沒送機，我就已經開始哭了」，並笑稱，若兒子讀書的地方太悶，自己去陪一星期就會回來，流露出為人之母的真性情。
除了感性話題，陳慧琳還分享，最近趕潮流用「AI 起紫微斗數命盤」的趣事。她不僅用AI幫兒子分析大學選科與溫習功課，還忍不住順便算了兒子的未來姻緣。她笑稱，AI分析結果顯示，兒子未來會找到一位賢淑、懂照顧人且與他十分合拍的伴侶，讓她很放心。幽默的「奶奶視角」成為全場訪問的輕鬆亮點。
現年54歲的陳慧琳還爆料，正值青春期的長子已開始拍拖，甚至向爸爸劉建浩請教追女生的祕訣。
談到張家輝憑《絕命法官》奪得「第31屆亞洲電視大獎」視帝，並將於黃曆新年舉行紅館演唱會，作為同門師姐（因陳慧琳入行並簽約鍾珍的時間較早，因此她常笑稱現年61歲的張家輝及其電影角色「蔡辛強」是自己的「首席師弟」）的陳慧琳表示，一定會到場支持。但她開玩笑說，擔心張家輝在電影《贖夢》中的分身角色「蔡辛強」天天練歌練舞，會搶走她的演唱會嘉賓位置，讓她沒機會上台向觀眾討紅包。
陳慧琳1995年出道即走紅，是香港娛樂圈「演歌雙棲」的指標性天后。她不僅在樂壇橫掃最高榮譽，也在影壇留下《無間道》等多部票房與口碑俱佳的作品，橫跨警匪、動作、愛情與奇幻題材，多部作品成為港產片代表。

content:
【大紀元2026年11月24日訊】（大紀元記者程木蘭、駱亞採訪報導）美中科技圍堵與芯片爭奪戰持續升級，一條橫跨美、星、馬及柬埔寨的英偉達（NVIDIA）高階人工智能芯片非法走私鏈近日遭媒體起底。這套由跨國洗錢集團、離岸雲端外衣與中國科技資本串聯的地下算力輸送網，不僅規避美國出口禁令獲取數十億美元暴利，更揭示北京當局透過「軍民融合」體系突破技術封鎖的黑幕。
英偉達董事會於11月23日一致通過讓黃仁勳即刻恢復總裁、執行長（CEO）及董事職務，結束11天高層變動。但高階芯片外流調查並未出爐。
這場震撼全球半導體產業界的風暴，始於黃仁勳因婚外情而於12日辭職，其涉嫌對象正是曾任新加坡雲端業者Megaspeed高層、捲入跨國芯片走私案的中國籍女子黃樂（Alice Huang）。
然而《華爾街日報》引述知情人士披露，具香港居留身分、英文流利的黃樂僅是面對西方市場的對外門面，幕後真正核心操盤手，實為現年52歲、暫獲保釋並居於中共駐新加坡大使館鄰近豪宅的中國籍男子李明。
根據新加坡檢方在2025年2月提出的詐欺起訴書，李明向美國供應商謊稱採購的硬體供星國公司Luxuriate Your Life使用，實則私運至馬來西亞並轉往未具名的第三地。
針對跨國企業如何穿透監管審查，美國經濟學者黃大衛接受大紀元採訪時直言，事件最關鍵的特徵在於「真正的生意與涉嫌走私之間的交易可以同時存在」。
黃大衛指出，Megaspeed確實經營海外雲端業務，並能以馬來西亞機房及中國電商巨擘阿里巴巴的合法租賃合約爭取英偉達供貨，「但一家雲端公司有真客戶，不代表他買的每台伺服器都留在他申報的機房」。
他分析，第一手交貨地點看似合法合規，後面卻進行轉運，暴露英偉達與供應鏈在查核「買家與用家是否為同一人」上的巨大管理漏洞。
台灣南華大學國際事務與企業學系教授孫國祥在受訪時也指出，此案凸顯當前跨國芯片走私已不再是單純的黑市買賣，而是演變成利用合法商業體系與非法網絡深度交織的「混合式供應鏈」。
孫國祥認為，走私集團以正常商業需求掩護實際貨物流向，導致合法交易與非法轉運之間的界限極其模糊，使美方出口管制政策面臨「第三地轉運、最終用戶查核與跨境執法」的三重嚴峻挑戰。
要將列管的尖端處理器運往中國，走私網絡首先必須建立合法的採購途徑。《金融時報》訪問 10多名知情人士與查閱數百份企業申報文件調查指出，整個供應鏈需要三個關鍵環節；國防安全學者沈明室亦向大紀元記者剖析，走私網絡正是由內而外分為三個圈層。
沈明室指出，第一環正是「合法供應商或白手套採購」。據《金融時報》報導，中國伺服器大廠浪潮集團（Inspur）雖於2023年3月因涉嫌協助軍方而被列入美國出口管制實體清單，但其設於加州聖荷西且未受制裁的美國子公司改名為Aivres後，仍保留向英偉達採購並組裝伺服器的資格。儘管英偉達內部曾質疑Aivres的資格，最終仍認定其符合法規要求；Aivres隨即成為向境外輸送算力硬體的源頭破口。
走私體系的第二環，則是於東南亞設立合規買家。《華爾街日報》與《金融時報》皆披露，2022年8月拜登政府限制向中國出口A100等芯片後，李明、黃樂與其丈夫康偉等人收購了中資遊戲公司第七大道的離岸部門，並將其包裝成新興雲端服務商Megaspeed。這家公司以黃樂無瑕的背景做為代表，於2023年11月順利躋身英偉達雲端合作夥伴計劃，取得優先配貨特權。
根據貿易數據平台ImportGenius的資料，僅2024年12月至2025年12月1年間，Megaspeed馬來西亞子公司Speedmatrix向Aivres進口的設備申報總值就高達約46億美元。
儘管英偉達在2025年6月在美國與新加坡展開調查之際將Megaspeed及其子公司列入禁售名單，黃樂亦於同年8月離職並遭新加坡當局限制入境，但幕後集團隨即展開「金蟬脫殼」。
《華爾街日報》查閱貨運記錄進一步披露，李明等原班團隊於2025年迅速成立新雲端公司 Novagate Cloud，該公司網站甚至宣稱取得英偉達最先進Blackwell芯片支援兩座資料中心；光是今年前5個月，Novagate馬來西亞實體再度接獲價值至少3億美元的英偉達硬體設備。放空機構Culper Research於5月發布報告，揭發Novagate網站結構與董事登記地址皆與Megaspeed如出一轍，顯示防堵機制在多層空殼公司替換下持續失靈。
這場跨國算力走私之所以能調動巨額資金並穿越邊境，關鍵在於第三環的地下物流與資金迴流。調查證實，因涉嫌跨國網絡投資詐騙、人口販運與洗錢而遭美、英、台多國執法打擊的柬埔寨「太子集團」（Prince Group），深度捲入了芯片交易。國際戰略研究所（IISS）研究員克拉格（Chris Clague）指出：「從供應鏈結構來看，走私芯片與走私毒品或武器沒有兩樣。」
《金融時報》調查指出，被美國當局指控為太子集團「二把手」的胡小偉（正式姓名An Ming Wu，1982年生，今年6月在日本被捕）是走私鏈的核心要角。雖然太子集團發言人全盤否認指控，但據調查，胡小偉早年藉由線上遊戲《熱血傳奇》私服與賭博累積財富，並與世紀華通董事長王佶等高層存在長年股權聯繫。
受訪學者黃大衛與孫國祥都認為，犯罪集團看中的是芯片短缺產生的巨大差價暴利，因此將長期服務於博弈、詐騙與虛擬貨幣的洗錢暗網，順理成章轉化為高科技走私的融資基底。沈明室進一步說明，太子集團利用數百間空殼公司及虛擬貨幣將非法資金洗白，藉以支付採購芯片的巨額貨款。
在實體運輸環節，走私網絡更動用了極其隱密的空中走廊。據披露，太子集團涉嫌利用胡小偉在香港設立的飛機租賃公司購買商務噴射機與私人飛機，將滯留於東南亞的受管制高階芯片空運偷渡進中國，藉此避開各國海關的常規查緝。據新加坡《海峽時報》報導，印尼警方於 2026年初突擊搜查Megaspeed當地設施時，赫然發現伺服器機架內早已空空如也，珍貴的GPU全數不翼而飛。
進入中國境內的走私芯片，隨即在黑市以原價數倍的高價迅速分流。知情人士指出，上海世紀利通是關鍵的分銷樞紐，科技媒體The Information率先報導了世紀利通在中國英偉達芯片交易網絡扮演的角色；該公司正是由黃樂家族與世紀華通合資的「世紀龍騰」所設立。儘管美國祭出嚴格管制，但彭博查閱的文件顯示，在上海與世紀龍騰關聯的數據中心內，確實安裝了受限的英偉達芯片。《金融時報》更披露，在美國收緊H20芯片管制後的短短3個月內，中國黑市便迅速消化售出價值至少10億美元的走私英偉達產品。
龐大的空殼架構除了逃避制裁，更在走私鏈與中國本土科技巨頭之間築起防護牆。調查指，世紀華通背後擁有騰訊（持股10.1%）與阿里巴巴的深度業務交集，三方甚至共同投資網約車平台T3出行，黃樂亦名列該平台董事。
雖然《金融時報》未發現證據顯示騰訊或阿里巴巴參與走私，騰訊極力澄清僅為少數股東投資，阿里巴巴亦未予置評，但沈明室點出，中國科技大廠與遊戲巨頭在背後扮演著至關重要的市場吸納角色，透過離岸算力租賃與境內轉售，支撐其龐大的AI基礎設施運作。
走私網絡最令國際情報與國安體系震驚的去向，是流入中共的國防科技與軍事研究機構。據調查披露，採購分銷網絡背後潛藏高達約幾十億美元的中共官方資金流向，相關企業母公司更曾向解放軍提供飛彈與戰機零件，存在廣泛股權與業務關聯。沈明室認為，合理推斷，這些芯片提供給中共軍工或國防體系是肯定的。
調查發現，部分受管制芯片已透過海外算力租賃與層層轉包，並流向從事軍事網絡戰的「之江實驗室」。
沈明室透露，中共國安部內部甚至特別成立了「人工智能小組」執行反封鎖行動，藉由各類走私進口的芯片協助本土機構訓練高階AI模型，不僅用於突破半導體封鎖，更實質投入於武器研發與軍事戰略模擬。
黃大衛引述路透社報導補充，具中共國防科研背景的西北工業大學，近期同樣被查出成功向供應商採購受嚴格管制的H200芯片。
他直言，當受監管的大學院校都能輕易透過管道取得高階芯片，反推軍方與情報體系早已利用此類網絡掌握所需算力，美國的防堵措施實質上僅增加了中方獲取技術的經濟成本，卻未能徹底切斷其算力獲取途徑。
